To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the distribution of renal cortical flow during autoregulation and acetylcholine vasodilation is similar, but that the pattern of redistribution during ethacrynic-induced diuresis is different.

the distribution of cortical flow during acetylcholine-induced renal vasodilation is similar to that observed during reduction of perfusion, and different from that observed during ethacrynic-acid-induced vasodilation.
the distribution of cortical flow is altered in different ways during renal vasodilatation induced by different stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the distribution of blood flow in the renal cortex during vasodilation induced in four different ways: by reducing perfusion pressure, by infusion of acetyl choline, by ethacry nic acid-induced diuresi and by mannitol-induced diuresi.
the mechanism of the heterogeneous cortical response to acetylcholine and autoregulation.
the distribution of cortical perfusion in response to different stimuli and the factors responsible for this distribution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
renal autoregulatory mechanisms are heterogeneous, and are differentially expressed in the superficial and juxtamedullar cortex.
the cortical distribution of blood flow is altered during renal vasodilatation by a number of different mechanisms, but the exact mechanism(s) responsible for this redistribution is/are not known.
the cortical distribution of flow is altered during renal vasodilatation, and that the pattern of redistribution is stimulus-specific, but not flow-specific.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
renal vasodilation is associated with a redistribution of cortical blood flow, which may be heterogeneous in nature.

acetylcholine and reduced renal perfusion pressure cause redistribution of renal cortical bloodflow to the deep cortex, whereas ethacrynic and mannitol diuresises cause redistribution to the middle cortex.

acetylcholine and reduction of perfusion pres-sure redistribute flow in the same manner because they both act on the same mechanism, autoregulation; and that ethacrynic-induced redistribution is a separate phenomenon.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution of flow in the renal cortex is heterogeneous and that this heterogeneity can be altered by different maneuvers.
the distribution of cortical perfusion is not uniform and that it can be changed by different maneuvers, such as autoregulation and acetylcholine infusion.

acetylcholine and autoregulatory responses redistribute cortical blood flow in similar fashion, suggesting that acetylcholinerelated vasodilation may be a major component of autoregulation in the dog kidney.
